title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 8

question.stem: The nurse reviews the ED flowsheet. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.
question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Highlight these nine findings: temperature 35.6° C; heart rate 116/min; blood pressure 96/58 lying and 80/50 mm Hg standing with dizziness; 100 mL of dark amber urine in 8 hours; erythema with scaling over about 90% of the body; potassium 3.1 mmol/L; magnesium 0.62 mmol/L; creatinine 132 µmol/L (84 three months ago); albumin 26 g/L.

Why these findings

  • Temperature 35.6° C: impaired thermoregulation; inflamed, dilated skin over 90% of the body loses heat. The nurse monitors temperature and provides warming measures.
  • Tachycardia; hypotension with an orthostatic drop: hemodynamic instability from fluid lost through the damaged skin. Hemodynamic stability is the priority in erythroderma.
  • 100 mL of urine in 8 hours: about 0.14 mL/kg/h in a 92-kg client: oliguria from hypovolemia.
  • Erythema over about 90% of the body: meets the definition of generalized exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma), a life-threatening condition managed in hospital.
  • Low potassium and magnesium: both raise the risk of dysrhythmias and are replaced; heavy alcohol use contributes to low magnesium.
  • Creatinine up from 84 to 132 µmol/L: suggests prerenal acute kidney injury from hypovolemia.
  • Albumin 26 g/L: protein lost through the shedding, inflamed skin. Low oncotic pressure explains the ankle edema.

Why the others are not urgent

  • RR 18/min and SpO2 97%: within normal limits.
  • Nail pitting and ridging: a chronic finding of nail psoriasis.
  • ESR 48 mm/h: elevated ESR is expected with psoriatic inflammation; monitor.
  • Hemoglobin 124 g/L: mild anemia, which can occur in erythroderma; not immediately dangerous.
  • ALT 34 U/L: normal, and a useful baseline before systemic therapy.

Stopped methotrexate 6 weeks ago after being laid off and losing his drug coverage. leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 54-year-old male client with plaque psoriasis progressing to generalized exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma).

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's hypotension and tachycardia are most likely caused by [[drop0]] as evidenced by [[drop1]]. His temperature of 35.6° C is most likely due to [[drop2]]. The bilateral ankle edema is most likely related to [[drop3]]. The flare was most likely triggered by [[drop4]].

options.text: fluid loss through the widely inflamed, shedding skin
the orthostatic blood pressure drop, dry oral mucosa, and low, concentrated urine output
a normal evening drop in body temperature
heat loss through widespread, dilated skin blood vessels
a low serum albumin from protein loss through the skin
stopping methotrexate, finishing a course of oral prednisone, heavy alcohol use, and stress

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 1 — Emergency Department, 2140. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 2140.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: The client's hypotension and tachycardia are most likely caused by fluid loss through the widely inflamed, shedding skin as evidenced by the orthostatic blood pressure drop, dry oral mucosa, and low, concentrated urine output. His temperature of 35.6° C is most likely due to heat loss through widespread, dilated skin blood vessels. The bilateral ankle edema is most likely related to a low serum albumin from protein loss through the skin. The flare was most likely triggered by stopping methotrexate, finishing a course of oral prednisone, heavy alcohol use, and stress.

Why

  • Fluid loss through the skin: in erythroderma the skin barrier is almost completely absent, so fluid is lost continuously. The orthostatic drop, dry mucosa and low, concentrated urine confirm volume depletion. A normal SpO2 and clear lungs argue against a cardiac cause, and there was no allergen exposure suggesting anaphylaxis. Nail pitting, the ESR and the SpO2 do not show volume status.
  • Heat loss through dilated skin vessels: inflamed, vasodilated skin over 90% of the body loses heat rapidly. He has not stopped drinking long enough for significant withdrawal, and alcohol withdrawal tends to raise temperature, not lower it.
  • Low albumin: albumin 26 g/L shows protein lost through scaling and exudation. Low oncotic pressure lets fluid shift into the tissues even while he is intravascularly depleted. No IV fluids have been given yet, and nothing suggests heart failure or bilateral DVT.
  • Triggers: stress and excessive alcohol are psoriasis triggers, and psoriasis is a contributing cause of erythroderma. Abruptly stopping systemic therapy and withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids are well-recognized triggers of erythrodermic flares. A streptococcal throat infection classically triggers guttate psoriasis, and detergents trigger contact dermatitis.

Beyond the chapter: methotrexate and corticosteroid withdrawal as triggers are standard dermatology content.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 54-year-old male client with plaque psoriasis progressing to generalized exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma).

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The priority nursing hypothesis at this time is [[drop0]] because [[drop1]]. Once this is addressed, the nurse's next priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: risk for hemodynamic instability related to fluid and electrolyte loss
the skin barrier is almost completely absent, allowing ongoing loss of fluid, protein, electrolytes, and heat

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: The priority nursing hypothesis at this time is risk for hemodynamic instability related to fluid and electrolyte loss because the skin barrier is almost completely absent, allowing ongoing loss of fluid, protein, electrolytes, and heat. Once this is addressed, the nurse's next priority is impaired skin integrity.

Why

  • Hemodynamic instability first: for ordinary plaque psoriasis, impaired skin integrity is the priority. Once the disease becomes erythroderma, the priority shifts to hemodynamic stability because the skin barrier is almost completely absent.
  • Loss of the skin barrier: this is the mechanism that makes erythroderma life-threatening. That psoriasis is autoimmune, that he stopped methotrexate and that the ESR is raised are all true, but they do not explain the immediate danger.
  • Impaired skin integrity next: the next hypothesis in erythroderma. Body image, knowledge and coping are real needs (he is tearful and isolating) and are addressed once he is physiologically stable.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 54-year-old male client with plaque psoriasis progressing to generalized exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma).

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care for the first 24 hours? Select all that apply.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to 1 L/day to reduce the ankle edema
Maintain strict intake and output and obtain a daily weight
Administer IV isotonic fluids as prescribed
Arrange an ultraviolet phototherapy session for tomorrow
Administer the prescribed oral antihistamine, preferably at bedtime
Replace potassium and magnesium as prescribed, with cardiac monitoring
Use hot water and a washcloth to scrub off loose scale
Provide lukewarm oatmeal soaks followed by a bland, oil-based emollient
Monitor for alcohol withdrawal using a validated scale (e.g., CIWA-Ar)
Apply coal tar ointment to all reddened skin
Keep the room warm, apply warm blankets, and monitor temperature frequently

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answers: IV isotonic fluids (Option 3); potassium and magnesium replacement with cardiac monitoring (Option 6); warm room, warm blankets and frequent temperature checks (Option 11); strict intake and output and daily weight (Option 2); lukewarm oatmeal soaks and a bland, oil-based emollient (Option 8); an oral antihistamine at bedtime (Option 5); and alcohol-withdrawal monitoring with a validated scale (Option 9).

Why these

  • IV isotonic fluids (Option 3): adequate hydration through IV fluid replacement maintains hemodynamic stability.
  • Potassium and magnesium (Option 6): potassium, magnesium and calcium are replaced when indicated; low potassium and magnesium raise the risk of dysrhythmias, so cardiac monitoring is prudent.
  • Warming (Option 11): frequent temperature checks with warming measures address impaired thermoregulation.
  • Intake and output, daily weight (Option 2): track the response to fluid replacement and ongoing losses.
  • Oatmeal soaks and emollient (Option 8): oatmeal baths soothe erythroderma and oil-based emollients help psoriasis; lukewarm water avoids more vasodilation and heat loss.
  • Bedtime antihistamine (Option 5): oral antihistamines (for example diphenhydramine) relieve itching; bedtime dosing uses the sedating effect. Supervise getting up because of the orthostatic hypotension.
  • Alcohol-withdrawal monitoring (Option 9): he drinks 6 to 8 beers a day; withdrawal can begin 6 to 24 hours after the last drink and would worsen his hemodynamic instability.

Why not the others

  • Fluid restriction (Option 1): the edema comes from low albumin while he is intravascularly depleted; restricting fluids would worsen the hypotension and kidney injury.
  • Coal tar on all reddened skin (Option 10): coal tar treats mild, localized psoriasis. On inflamed, broken skin over 90% of the body it irritates and can worsen erythroderma.
  • Phototherapy (Option 4): used for stable psoriasis; ultraviolet light on acutely inflamed skin can aggravate erythroderma, and he is unstable.
  • Hot water and scrubbing (Option 7): friction and heat further damage the fragile barrier, increase heat and fluid loss, and invite infection.

Beyond the chapter: alcohol-withdrawal monitoring and the coal tar contraindication in erythroderma are standard content.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 54-year-old male client with plaque psoriasis progressing to generalized exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for the client on hospital day 3.

rows.text: Confirm that the TB and hepatitis screening results are documented before the first infliximab infusion
Monitor vital signs and observe for an infusion reaction (fever, chills, dyspnea, hives) during and after the infusion
Teach the client to report fever, cough, night sweats, or signs of skin infection promptly
Advise the client to get any overdue live vaccines (e.g., MMR) now that infusions are starting
Explain that the infusions can be stopped once his skin clears
Refer the client to a social worker for drug-coverage options and to a psoriasis support group or counselling
Teach stress-reduction strategies and support his plan to reduce alcohol intake
Encourage long, hot showers to soften and remove scale

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 2 — Medical Unit, Hospital Day 3. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Hospital Day 3 and the Screening Results.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Indicated: confirm the TB and hepatitis screening before the first infusion; monitor vital signs and watch for an infusion reaction; teach him to report fever, cough, night sweats or skin infection; refer to a social worker and a psoriasis support group or counselling; teach stress reduction and support his plan to cut down on alcohol.
  • Contraindicated: advising overdue live vaccines now; explaining that infusions can stop once the skin clears; encouraging long, hot showers.

Why

  • TB and hepatitis screening: with systemic and biologic therapy (infliximab is one), the nurse monitors for serious infections such as tuberculosis and hepatitis. TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent TB and hepatitis B, so negative screening is confirmed first.
  • Infusion reaction: infliximab can cause fever, chills, dyspnea, hives or hypotension during or after the infusion.
  • Infection warning signs: suppressed immunity makes infection more likely.
  • Live vaccines (contraindicated): live vaccines are avoided during biologic immunosuppression; needed vaccines are given before therapy starts, per the prescriber.
  • Stopping once the skin clears (contraindicated): psoriasis is chronic, with remissions and relapses; the nurse reinforces adherence. Stopping therapy is what caused this admission.
  • Social work and support group: address the root cause of his non-adherence (lost drug coverage) and the psychosocial impact of his skin disease.
  • Stress and alcohol reduction: stress and excessive alcohol are psoriasis triggers.
  • Long, hot showers (contraindicated): heat and prolonged water exposure dry and irritate the skin and promote heat and fluid loss; lukewarm soaks followed by emollients are used instead.

Beyond the chapter: infusion reactions and live-vaccine precautions are standard pharmacology.

question.stem: For each finding on hospital day 7, click to specify whether it indicates that the plan of care has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: BP 124/78 mm Hg and HR 82 beats/min, with no orthostatic change
Erythema reduced to about 40% of the body; less peeling; itch rated 3/10
Excoriation on the right shin now has a honey-coloured crust with surrounding redness and warmth
Alcohol withdrawal scores 0–2 for the past 72 hours
Client states: “If my skin stays clear, I'll just skip the next infusion.”

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 3 — Medical Unit, Hospital Day 7. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Hospital Day 7.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Effective: BP 124/78 mm Hg and HR 82 beats/min with no orthostatic change; temperature 36.8° C; potassium 4.1 and magnesium 0.84 mmol/L; erythema down to about 40% with less peeling and itch 3/10; alcohol-withdrawal scores 0 to 2.
  • Not effective: the honey-coloured crust with redness and warmth on the right shin; the plan to skip the next infusion.

Why

  • Stable BP and HR: meets the outcome of vital signs within normal limits without fluid imbalance.
  • Temperature 36.8° C: thermoregulation restored.
  • Normal potassium and magnesium: no electrolyte disturbance.
  • Less erythema, peeling and itch: the skin is beginning to heal.
  • Honey-coloured crust with redness and warmth: a classic sign of secondary bacterial infection; yellow crusts over excoriations signal infection. The nurse notifies the provider (topical mupirocin is commonly prescribed); infection risk is higher on a biologic.
  • Withdrawal scores 0 to 2: withdrawal was prevented or managed.
  • "I'll just skip the next infusion": the adherence teaching has not been understood. The nurse evaluates the education and reinforces continuing treatment.
